summary: States the IETF's position on building wiretapping capability into IETF standards-track protocols. It explains what the question means, why the answer is no, and what that answer implies. It is an informational statement of policy rather than a technical specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A group that designs the rules of the road decided not to build secret listening tools into the road system. This note explains why they said no.

questions: does the ietf support wiretapping in protocols
what is the raven process ietf
subtitle: The IETF and IAB explain why wiretapping features will not be designed into IETF standards.

tldr.problem: The IETF was asked to take a position on adding functionality to standards-track documents to make wiretapping easier, a question that came up in work on IP-based telephony.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB and IESG define wiretapping precisely, review the discussion that led to the question, and conclude that the IETF will not consider wiretapping requirements when creating or maintaining its standards.
tldr.outcome: The memo gives five reasons, including that such features add complexity and lower the security of a system, and it says wiretapping mechanisms that do exist should be openly described.

today: RFC 2804 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records the IETF's stated policy as of May 2000.

sections.title: The Summary Position
sections.content:
This policy memo comes from the IAB and the IESG. The IETF decided not to consider requirements for wiretapping as part of the process of creating and maintaining IETF standards. It gives several reasons.

  • The IETF is an international body and the wrong forum for features driven by the laws of individual countries, which vary widely. Bodies tied to a single jurisdiction are more appropriate.
  • Internet traffic crosses networks run under many jurisdictions with different privacy requirements, so the security properties of connections should be as well known and as free from loopholes as possible.
  • Traffic not protected by the end systems can already be wiretapped with existing network features. The IETF sees no engineering solution that allows wiretapping when end systems protect their communications adequately.
  • Adding a wiretapping requirement makes protocol designs considerably more complex, and complexity almost inevitably jeopardizes security. The wiretap access itself must also be protected.
  • The IETF restates its belief, set out in RFC 1984, that commercial development of the Internet and adequate privacy for users need wide availability of strong cryptographic technology.

On the other hand, mechanisms that facilitate wiretapping, and known weaknesses in them, should be openly described so they get the maximum review. The IETF calls publishing them a Good Thing.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule makers said they would not add secret listening features, and explained why. They did say that if anyone builds such features, they should show everyone how they work.

sections.title: The Raven Process
sections.content:
The question arose from IETF work on IP-based telephony. In the telephone world, equipment makers and law enforcement have a tradition of cooperating on wiretapping, often required by law, and some telephony standards bodies added intercept features to their standards.

A working group developing a standard for communication between components of a distributed phone switch raised the issue. Because the IETF had never done this kind of work, its management held a public discussion first and created the Raven mailing list. Close to 500 people subscribed and about 10% of them sent at least one message.

The discussion continued at an IETF plenary in Washington, D.C., where twenty-nine people spoke. Opinions ranged from 'governments have no right to wiretap' to 'it will be done somewhere, best have it done where the technology was developed'. In a show of hands, very few spoke strongly for adding intercept features and many spoke against, but a sizable part of the audience abstained. The IESG and IAB were then asked to formulate a policy.
sections.plainLanguage: People first argued about it by email and then in a big room. Most who spoke did not want it, and many did not pick a side, so the leaders wrote down a policy.

sections.title: What Counts as Wiretapping
sections.content:
The memo says legal definitions are not precise enough at the technical level, so it defines wiretapping itself. It is what occurs when information passed across the Internet from one party to others is delivered to a third party, and all four of these hold:

  1. The sending party does not know about the third party.
  2. None of the recipients know about the delivery.
  3. The sender normally expects only the recipients, or parties obliged to keep it confidential, to see the information.
  4. The third party acts deliberately to target that transmission.

So monitoring public newsgroups is not wiretapping (condition 3 fails), random monitoring of a large population is not (condition 4 fails), and a recipient passing on private email is not (condition 2 fails). Call tracing through accounting logs, sometimes called pen registers, does count.

The memo splits wiretapping into three steps: capture, filtering and delivery. The definition deliberately ignores whether the tap is legal, whether it happens in real time, and which medium is targeted. The IETF takes no moral position, because there is no consensus on one and no way to detect the morality of an act on the wire. It does observe that tools effective for a purpose tend to be used for it, and for other purposes too.
sections.plainLanguage: Secretly listening only counts if the people talking do not know, the listener is aimed at them on purpose, and they expected privacy. Reading a public notice board does not count.

sections.title: How Useful Is Wiretapping on the Internet
sections.content:
The memo makes some general observations, noting that no specific proposals are being developed in the IETF. Copying the bytes between two users with known, static points of attachment is not hard, and standard diagnostic functions can do it. Linking identities to points of attachment is harder, because it means working with the subsystems for address assignment and name resolution.

An adversary also has simple countermeasures even without encryption, such as Internet cafes, anonymous dialups, anonymous remailers and multi-hop login sessions. Traffic protected by strong encryption can be recorded, but its content stays unavailable, leaving only traffic analysis.

The conclusion is that wiretapping works well when the target is ignorant or believes himself innocent, but Internet-based wiretapping is less useful than might be imagined against an alerted and technically competent adversary.
sections.plainLanguage: Listening in is easy on people who are not being careful, but people who know what they are doing have many ways to dodge it, like locking their messages in a box.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
By definition, wiretapping releases information the sender did not expect to be released. A system that allows it must therefore contain a function that can be used without alerting the sender, so the system cannot guarantee privacy; at most it can guarantee it as long as the wiretap function is not used. The memo gives the example that encrypted telephone conferences would have to hide from participants to whom any shared keying material is being revealed.

Such a system is less secure and more complex than it could be without the function, and the added complexity raises the risk of unintended security flaws. Wiretapping, even when it is not being exercised, therefore lowers the security of the system.
sections.plainLanguage: A secret door in a house that you promise not to use is still a door someone could open, so the house is less safe even when nobody opens it.

references.text: IAB and IESG, "IAB and IESG Statement on Cryptographic Technology and the Internet", RFC 1984, August 1996.
